items.title: Origin & Founder of Buddhism
items.body:
## History & Origin

- **Buddhism arose ~2,600 years ago** in India as a **spiritual path to overcome suffering and attain enlightenment**; it remains one of the most significant religions of **South and Southeast Asia**.
- Its founder was **Siddhartha Gautama**, born in **563 BCE**, also known as **Sakyamuni** and **Tathagata**.
- He belonged to the **Sakya clan of Kapilvastu** (modern-day **Lumbini, Nepal**).
- His parents were **King Suddhodana** and **Queen Mahamaya**.

The historical Buddha is thus rooted in the 6th-century-BCE Gangetic world, and his teachings later spread across Asia through the Sangha and royal patronage.

figure.alt: Artistic serene portrait of the meditating Gautama Buddha with closed eyes
figure.caption: Siddhartha Gautama (563 BCE) — the Sakyamuni, founder of Buddhism, born to King Suddhodana and Queen Mahamaya of the Sakya clan.

keyPoints: Founder: Siddhartha Gautama, born 563 BCE; also called Sakyamuni and Tathagata.
Born into the Sakya clan of Kapilvastu (modern Lumbini, Nepal).
Parents: King Suddhodana and Queen Mahamaya.
Buddhism arose ~2,600 years ago as a path to overcome suffering and attain enlightenment.
Major religion of South and Southeast Asia.
items.mnemonic: Founder facts — "563-ST": born 563 BCE, Sakyamuni & Tathagata, of the Sakya clan.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (History & Origin of Buddhism)

items.title: Early Life & the Four Great Sights
items.body:
## The Early Life of Siddhartha Gautama

- Siddhartha lived a **luxurious life as a prince**, but was **deeply disturbed** by the suffering he witnessed — the **Four Great Sights**:
  1. **A corpse** (dead body)
  2. **An old man** (old age)
  3. **A sick man** (disease)
  4. **A world renouncer / ascetic**
- At the age of **29**, he **renounced his royal life** and adopted the path of **asceticism** (extreme self-discipline).
- He spent **six years** practising **severe austerities**, seeking the truth about suffering and its causes.

The sight of ageing, disease and death, contrasted with the calm of the renouncer, set him on the quest that would end in enlightenment.

figure.alt: Serene painted portrait of the Buddha in meditation
figure.caption: The Four Great Sights — an old man, a sick man, a corpse and an ascetic — moved the prince to renounce palace life at the age of 29.

keyPoints: Four Great Sights that disturbed the prince: a corpse, an old man, a sick man, and a world renouncer.
Renounced royal life at the age of 29 (the Great Departure).
Adopted asceticism — extreme self-discipline.
Practised severe austerities for six years seeking the truth about suffering.
The sights symbolise old age, disease, death and the ascetic path out of suffering.
items.mnemonic: Four Sights — "OSCA": Old man → Sick man → Corpse → Ascetic (renouncer).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (The Early Life of Siddhartha Gautama)

items.title: Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya
items.body:
## Enlightenment (Bodhi)

- After **renouncing severe asceticism**, Siddhartha **meditated under a pipal tree** (later the **Bodhi tree**) at **Bodhgaya, Bihar**.
- After **49 days of meditation**, he **attained Bodhi (enlightenment)** and became the **Buddha — 'the Enlightened One'**.
- The pipal tree thereafter became the **Bodhi Tree**, a **symbol of Buddhist enlightenment**.

Abandoning both palace luxury and extreme austerity, the enlightenment marks the discovery of the **Middle Path** and the birth of Buddhism proper.
keyPoints: Meditated under a pipal tree (later the Bodhi tree) at Bodhgaya, Bihar.
Attained Bodhi (enlightenment) after 49 days of meditation.
Became the Buddha — 'the Enlightened One'.
The pipal tree became the Bodhi Tree, symbol of Buddhist enlightenment.
Enlightenment followed his renunciation of severe asceticism.
Enlightenment came under a pipal (Bodhi) tree at Bodh Gaya on the bank of the Niranjana (Falgu) river.
items.mnemonic: Enlightenment — "49 under the pipal at Bodh Gaya = Bodhi".
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (Enlightenment)

items.title: First Sermon — Dharma-Chakra-Pravartana
items.body:
## Turning the Wheel of Law

- Buddha delivered his **first sermon at Sarnath, near Varanasi**, marking the **turning of the wheel of law** — this event is called **Dharma-Chakra-Pravartana**.
- In this sermon he introduced the **Four Noble Truths** and the **Eightfold Path** to his disciples.
- These teachings form the **foundation of Buddhist philosophy**.

Sarnath (the deer park) is therefore where Buddhism's core doctrine was first proclaimed.

figure.alt: Flowchart of the Four Noble Truths with their tasks, recognition and realization
figure.caption: At Sarnath (Dharma-Chakra-Pravartana) the Buddha first taught the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.

keyPoints: First sermon at Sarnath, near Varanasi.
The event is called Dharma-Chakra-Pravartana — 'turning the wheel of law'.
Introduced the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
These teachings form the foundation of Buddhist philosophy.
Delivered to his first disciples.
items.mnemonic: First Sermon = Sarnath = 'Dharma-Chakra-Pravartana' (turning the wheel of law).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (The First Sermon: Turning the Wheel of Law)

items.title: Mahaparinirvana at Kushinagar
items.body:
## Mahaparinirvana

- Buddha passed away at the age of **80**, in **483 BCE**, at **Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh**.
- His death is known as **Mahaparinirvana**, signifying his **final release from the cycle of rebirth**.

Kushinagar thus completes the four great life-places of the Buddha, alongside Lumbini (birth), Bodh Gaya (enlightenment) and Sarnath (first sermon).
keyPoints: Buddha died at age 80 in 483 BCE.
Place of death: Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh.
His death is called Mahaparinirvana.
Mahaparinirvana signifies final release from the cycle of rebirth.
Completes the four sacred life-places of the Buddha.
items.mnemonic: Mahaparinirvana — "80 in 483 BCE at Kushinagar = final release".
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (Mahaparinirvana)

items.title: Life-Events → Places (Quick Map)
items.body:
## Four Sacred Places in the Buddha's Life

| Event | Place | Region |
|---|---|---|
| **Birth** | **Lumbini** (Kapilvastu) | Nepal |
| **Enlightenment (Bodhi)** | **Bodh Gaya** | Bihar |
| **First Sermon** (Dharma-Chakra-Pravartana) | **Sarnath**, near Varanasi | Uttar Pradesh |
| **Mahaparinirvana (death)** | **Kushinagar** | Uttar Pradesh |

- These four events + places are the single most tested chain in the topic.
- Note the two **Nepal-linked** points (Lumbini birth, Sakya clan of Kapilvastu) versus the three sites in **India** (Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar).
keyPoints: Birth → Lumbini (Kapilvastu), Nepal.
Enlightenment → Bodh Gaya, Bihar.
First Sermon → Sarnath, near Varanasi.
Mahaparinirvana (death) → Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh.
Sarnath's event is named Dharma-Chakra-Pravartana.
items.mnemonic: Life-event → place — "LBSK": Lumbini (born), Bodh Gaya (enlightened), Sarnath (sermon), Kushinagar (death).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (Origin; Enlightenment; First Sermon; Mahaparinirvana)

items.title: Triratna — The Three Jewels
items.body:
## The Three Jewels (Three Refuges)

The **Triratna** are central to Buddhist practice, representing core values that guide practitioners toward enlightenment:

- **Buddha** — the ideal of **enlightenment**; the spiritual teacher and example of freedom from suffering and ignorance. Practitioners take refuge in the Buddha as inspiration for their inner potential.
- **Dharma** — the **teachings of the Buddha**; the path to enlightenment offering guidance for an ethical, mindful life. It is the truth, encompassing practices, moral codes and wisdom.
- **Sangha** — the **community of practitioners** (monks, nuns and lay followers) who support one another; it stresses the importance of community in spiritual progress.
keyPoints: Triratna = Buddha, Dharma, Sangha (the 'Three Jewels' / 'Three Refuges').
Buddha: the ideal and example of enlightenment.
Dharma: the teachings — the path to enlightenment and ethical living.
Sangha: the community of monks, nuns and lay followers.
Together they guide practitioners toward liberation.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (Three Jewels of Buddhism)

items.title: The Four Noble Truths (Ariya-Sacchani)
items.body:
## The Essence of the Buddha's Teaching

| Noble Truth | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Dukkha** (Truth of Suffering) | Life is full of suffering (**Sabbam Dukham**); suffering exists in every aspect of life. |
| **Samudaya** (Cause of Suffering) | The cause of suffering is **Trishna** (desire/craving), which leads to attachment and unhappiness. |
| **Nirodha** (End of Suffering) | Suffering can end by attaining **Nirvana / Nibbana** — the cessation of all desires and attachments. |
| **Ashtangika-Marga** (Path to End Suffering) | The **Eightfold Path** offers a practical guide to end suffering and achieve enlightenment. |

- The Four Noble Truths are collectively called the **Ariya-Sacchani**.
- Diagnosis → Cause → Cure → Path: suffering exists, has a cause (craving), can end (Nirvana), via the Path.

figure.alt: Colour flowchart of the Four Noble Truths showing the truth, origin, extinction and path relating to Dukkha
figure.caption: The Four Noble Truths (Ariya-Sacchani): Dukkha, Samudaya, Nirodha and Ashtangika-Marga.

keyPoints: Four Noble Truths = Ariya-Sacchani.
Dukkha: life is full of suffering (Sabbam Dukham).
Samudaya: cause of suffering is Trishna (desire/craving).
Nirodha: suffering ends by attaining Nirvana/Nibbana.
Ashtangika-Marga: the Eightfold Path is the way to end suffering.
items.mnemonic: Four Noble Truths — "D-S-N-M": Dukkha (suffering exists), Samudaya (craving causes it), Nirodha (it can end), Marga (via the Path).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (The Four Noble Truths — Ariya-Sacchani)

items.title: The Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga)
items.body:
## Eight Interconnected Practices

| Step | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Right Vision** (Samma Ditthi) | Understanding the true nature of reality and the path to transformation. |
| **Right Thought** (Samma Sankappa) | Thoughts of non-harm, compassion and love. |
| **Right Speech** (Samma Vacca) | Speaking truthfully and kindly, avoiding harmful words. |
| **Right Action** (Samma Kammanta) | Acting ethically — refraining from violence, stealing and immoral behaviour. |
| **Right Livelihood** (Samma Ajiva) | Earning a living without harming or exploiting others. |
| **Right Effort** (Samma Vayama) | Developing positive habits and eliminating negative tendencies. |
| **Right Mindfulness** (Samma Sati) | Awareness of body, mind and feelings; staying present. |
| **Right Concentration** (Samma Samadhi) | Deep meditative concentration to purify the mind and attain liberation. |

- The Eightfold Path (**Ashtangika Marga**) is the practical route to spiritual awakening and liberation from suffering.

figure.alt: Diagram of the Buddha's Eightfold Path listing the eight right practices with Pali names
figure.caption: The Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga) — eight interconnected practices leading to liberation.

keyPoints: Eightfold Path = Ashtangika Marga: eight interconnected practices to end suffering.
Right Vision (Samma Ditthi), Right Thought (Samma Sankappa), Right Speech (Samma Vacca), Right Action (Samma Kammanta).
Right Livelihood (Samma Ajiva), Right Effort (Samma Vayama), Right Mindfulness (Samma Sati), Right Concentration (Samma Samadhi).
It is the fourth Noble Truth (Ashtangika-Marga) in practice.
Goal: spiritual awakening and liberation from suffering.
items.mnemonic: Eightfold Path order — "V-T-S-A-L-E-M-C": Vision, Thought, Speech, Action, Livelihood, Effort, Mindfulness, Concentration.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (The Eightfold Path — Ashtangika Marga)

items.title: The Middle Path
items.body:
## The Middle Path (Madhyama Marga)

- Siddhartha first led a **luxurious life as a prince**, then swung to the opposite extreme — **six years of severe austerities** as an ascetic.
- Finding neither indulgence nor extreme self-mortification effective, he **renounced severe asceticism** and, meditating under the pipal tree at Bodh Gaya, attained enlightenment.
- This balanced route between **luxury and extreme austerity** is the **Middle Path** — realised in practice through the **Eightfold Path**.

The Middle Path is why the Buddha's method rejected both the pleasure-seeking of court life and the body-punishing austerity of contemporary ascetics.
keyPoints: Middle Path = the balanced route between palace luxury and extreme self-mortification.
The prince's luxurious life was one extreme; six years of severe austerities the other.
He renounced severe asceticism before attaining enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.
The Middle Path is realised in practice through the Eightfold Path.
It rejects both indulgence and extreme austerity.
items.mnemonic: Middle Path — 'neither the palace nor the penance': avoid luxury AND extreme austerity.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (Early Life; Enlightenment — renouncing severe asceticism)

items.title: Causes for the Rise of Buddhism
items.body:
## Why Buddhism Spread in the 6th Century BCE

- **Socio-Political Conditions:** people were frustrated by **Brahmanical rituals, superstitions and the complexities of Vedic religion**.
- **Simple Doctrines:** Buddhism offered easy teachings — the **Four Noble Truths** and **Eightfold Path** — accessible to the common people.
- **Language of the People:** Buddha taught in **Prakrit**, the language of the masses, unlike Vedic **Sanskrit** (restricted to Brahmins).
- **Personality of Buddha:** his **compassionate, kind demeanour** and **selfless actions** endeared him to people.
- **Absence of Caste Discrimination:** Buddhism **opposed the caste system**; people of all castes could join the **Sangha**.
keyPoints: Reaction against Brahmanical rituals, superstitions and Vedic complexity.
Simple doctrines: Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path, easy for common people.
Taught in Prakrit (people's language), not restricted Sanskrit.
Buddha's compassionate personality and selfless actions.
Opposed caste discrimination — all castes could join the Sangha.
items.mnemonic: Rise causes — "SSLPC": Simple doctrines, Socio-political frustration, Language (Prakrit), Personality, Caste-free Sangha.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (Causes for the Rise of Buddhism)

items.title: Key Concepts & Beliefs
items.body:
## Core Beliefs of Buddhism

- **Ahimsa (Non-Violence):** a central tenet — no harm to any living creature, extending to thoughts, words and actions.
- **Vegetarianism:** not strictly required, but many Buddhists adopt it as a reflection of non-violence and compassion.
- **No God or Soul:** Buddhism **rejects a creator god** and denies a permanent soul (**Atman**); existence is marked by **impermanence** and enlightenment comes from realising the **non-self (Anatman)**.
- **Criticism of the Varna System:** Buddha opposed social hierarchy based on birth and advocated **equality**, uplifting Shudras and women (who could join the Sangha on equal terms).
- **Overcoming Hatred with Love:** evil should be countered with goodness, hatred with love.
- **Redefined Varna:** emphasis on **Karma (actions)** and attributes rather than birth.
keyPoints: Ahimsa (non-violence) is a central tenet — extends to thought, word and action.
Rejects a creator God and a permanent soul (Atman); teaches impermanence and non-self (Anatman).
Liberation = Nirvana, the cessation of desire and attachment.
Opposed the varna/caste system; upheld equality for Shudras and women in the Sangha.
Redefined status by Karma (actions) and moral conduct, not birth.
items.mnemonic: Beliefs — "A-A-A": Ahimsa (non-violence), Anatman (no soul), Anti-caste (equality via Karma).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Buddhism I (Doctrines of Buddhism; Beliefs in Buddhism)

items.title: For Mains — Buddhism I (Life & Teachings)
items.body:
## How Mains frames the Buddha's teaching

Mains (Paper-II, clause M2-1) rarely asks for a bare biography; it asks you to *analyse* why a simple ethical doctrine became a world religion and a social reform movement. Treat the Four Truths/Eightfold Path as a **rational, this-worldly ethic** and connect it to its **social and historical impact**.

| Dimension | Analytical thrust |
|---|---|
| Causes | Reaction to Vedic ritualism and Brahmin monopoly; Second Urbanisation created a trader/gahapati class receptive to a casteless ethic |
| Doctrine | Four Noble Truths as a 'physician's diagnosis'; Middle Path as pragmatic rationalism; Pratityasamutpada (dependent origination) |
| Social radicalism | Open Sangha for all varnas, women (Bhikkhuni order); use of Prakrit/Pali vs Sanskrit |
| Impact | Growth of monasteries, trade-route patronage, Gandhara/Amaravati art, spread abroad |
| Limits/critique | Monastic rigidity, later ritualism and Mahayana image-worship diluted the original rationalism |

**Data points / anchors to quote:** life dates 563–483 BCE (traditional); First Sermon = Dharmachakrapravartana at Sarnath; patrons Bimbisara, Ajatashatru, later Ashoka and Kanishka; Pali Tripitaka as source; the trader/gahapati base of early Buddhism (R.S. Sharma, D.D. Kosambi); B.R. Ambedkar's *The Buddha and His Dhamma* (1956) and the Navayana conversion for modern relevance.

**AP angle:** Early Buddhism struck deep roots in Andhra — the **Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu, Ghantasala and Salihundam** stupas on the Krishna valley, patronised by the **Satavahanas and Ikshvakus**, and **Acharya Nagarjuna** (Madhyamaka philosophy) at Nagarjunakonda. A sentence on this is a reliable AP-specific mark.

**Use in answers:**
- *Thesis line:* "The Buddha offered an ethical, rational and casteless path that answered the social churn of the Second Urbanisation."
- *Diagram idea:* the diagnostic chain Dukkha → Samudaya → Nirodha → Marga (disease → cause → cure → treatment).
- *Quote:* Ambedkar on Buddhism as a religion of 'liberty, equality and fraternity'.
- Conclude with its civilisational legacy in art, education (Nalanda/Amaravati) and Asian cultural diplomacy.
keyPoints: Analyse why a simple ethic became a reform movement, not just a biography.
Link the open Sangha and Prakrit preaching to the Second Urbanisation's trader class.
Present the Four Noble Truths as a rational 'diagnosis-and-cure' ethic (Middle Path).
Cite Ambedkar's Navayana and the Pali Tripitaka for sources and modern relevance.
AP angle: Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu stupas and Acharya Nagarjuna on the Krishna valley.
items.source: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past; A.L. Basham, The Wonder That Was India; B.R. Ambedkar, The Buddha and His Dhamma
